answerKey.primaryProblem: Acute viral gastroenteritis with mild (early) dehydration in a 14-month-old
differential: Viral gastroenteritis (most likely, daycare contacts ill, vomiting then diarrhea pattern)
Bacterial gastroenteritis (less likely, no blood/mucus in stool, no high fever)
Intussusception (less likely, no bilious vomiting, no severe episodic pain, abdomen soft)
Urinary tract infection presenting with fever (less likely given clear GI prodrome and daycare exposure)
Toddler diarrhea from excess fruit juice (contributing factor given diluted apple juice intake, but doesn't explain fever/vomiting)
keyFindings: 2 days vomiting now resolving, 6 watery stools/day
Alert, consolable, tears present with crying, brisk cap refill and skin turgor - reassuring against moderate/severe dehydration
Dry/sticky mucous membranes - sign of mild dehydration
Mother gave one dose of adult loperamide - inappropriate and should be stopped
Daycare contacts with similar illness supports viral etiology
plan: Classify as mild dehydration based on exam (alert, tears, brisk cap refill, skin turgor normal) despite modest weight loss
Start oral rehydration solution (ORS) in small frequent amounts (5-10 mL every few minutes), especially after each loose stool or vomit
Continue age-appropriate diet/breastfeeding or regular milk once rehydrating; do not withhold food long-term
Advise against loperamide and any adult antidiarrheal/antiemetic medications in toddlers - counsel on risks (ileus, CNS depression) and instruct to discard remaining medication safely
Advise stopping diluted juice as primary fluid; juice can worsen osmotic diarrhea

Provide explicit return precautions: no urine output >8 hours, sunken eyes/fontanelle, lethargy, inability to keep fluids down, bilious/green vomiting, blood in stool, high fever, or if seems to be worsening - seek in-person/ER care
Plan reweigh in 24-48 hours (telehealth follow-up or in-person if available) to confirm response to rehydration
Reinforce hand hygiene and daycare exclusion per daycare/public health policy until symptoms resolve
redFlags: Signs of worsening dehydration: sunken fontanelle, no tears, dry mucous membranes progressing, decreased urine output further, lethargy, cool extremities, delayed cap refill
Bilious or persistently forceful vomiting (concern for obstruction/intussusception)
High or persistent fever not improving
Signs of intussusception: severe intermittent abdominal pain, drawing legs up, currant-jelly stools
Caregiver medication error (adult antidiarrheal given to toddler) needing correction
educationPoints: Oral rehydration solution is first-line for mild-moderate dehydration in children; small frequent volumes reduce vomiting risk
Loperamide and other antimotility/antidiarrheal agents are not recommended in young children due to risk of ileus, toxic megacolon, and CNS/respiratory depression
Fruit juice, especially apple juice, has high fructose/sorbitol content and can worsen osmotic diarrhea - should be limited during and after GI illness

Clinical hydration assessment (mental status, tears, mucous membranes, skin turgor, capillary refill) is more reliable than weight alone for grading dehydration severity in a single visit, though serial weights are useful to confirm improvement
Continuing age-appropriate feeding during diarrheal illness supports gut recovery and nutrition; prolonged fasting is not advised
Daycare outbreaks of viral gastroenteritis are common; hand hygiene and exclusion criteria help limit spread

cells: 3rd dose due at 6-18mo, not yet given
Due at 12-15 months, not yet given - discuss at next well visit

facts.chart: Mother reports 2 days of vomiting (now improving) and watery diarrhea, with low-grade fever
facts.says: He's been throwing up for a couple days and now he's got really watery poops, like six times a day. I'm worried he's getting dehydrated.

facts.says: It started two days ago, he threw up maybe four or five times that first day, but yesterday and today it's only happened once.

facts.chart: Vomitus non-bloody, non-bilious (no green color reported)
facts.says: It wasn't green or anything, just whatever he'd eaten, kind of milky looking.

facts.chart: 6 watery stools per day currently, no blood or mucus reported
facts.says: He's going about six times a day now, it's really watery, almost like water coming out of his diaper.

facts.chart: No blood or mucus noted in stool
facts.says: No blood that I've seen, no weird mucus stuff either, just watery and yellow-ish.

facts.chart: Low-grade fever, max 38.1C, intermittent
facts.says: He's had a bit of a fever, I checked it and it was like 38.1 at the highest, comes and goes.

facts.chart: Several children at daycare reportedly ill with similar symptoms
facts.says: A bunch of kids at his daycare have been sick with the same thing, throwing up and diarrhea, so I figured that's where he got it.

facts.chart: Taking small sips of fluid; tolerating small amounts without vomiting today
facts.says: He's drinking little bits here and there, not a lot, but he's keeping it down today at least.

facts.chart: 3 wet diapers in last 24 hours, down from usual 5-6; urine appears more concentrated
facts.says: I've only changed like three wet diapers today, usually it's more like five or six.

facts.chart: Alert and interactive between episodes, fussy but consolable, no lethargy
facts.says: He's cranky and clingy but when I pick him up he calms down, he's not just lying there limp or anything.

facts.chart: Tears present when crying
facts.says: When he cries he still has tears, I checked because I read that's a sign.

facts.chart: Weight 10.4 kg one week ago at well visit, 10.1 kg today on home scale
facts.says: At his checkup last week he was 10.4 kilos, and I weighed him this morning on our scale at home and it said 10.1.

facts.chart: Mother giving diluted apple juice; stopped regular whole milk during illness
facts.says: I've been giving him watered-down apple juice because I thought that would be gentle on his tummy, and I stopped the milk since I heard that can make diarrhea worse.

facts.chart: Mother administered one 2 mg dose of adult OTC loperamide (Imodium) to the child the day before this visit, from the home medicine cabinet
facts.says: I did give him one dose of that Imodium stuff we had in the cabinet, just a little bit, I figured it would help stop the diarrhea.

facts.chart: No apparent severe abdominal pain; mild fussiness with gas, no episodic doubling-over or leg-drawing
facts.says: He gets a little fussy and squirms sometimes, but he's not screaming in pain or pulling his legs up like something's really wrong.

facts.chart: No rash reported
facts.says: No rash that I've noticed anywhere on him.

facts.chart: No cough, no runny nose, no respiratory symptoms
facts.says: No cough or runny nose, nothing like that.

facts.chart: No ear pulling or signs of ear pain
facts.says: He's not tugging at his ears or anything like that.

facts.chart: No foul-smelling urine or apparent pain with urination reported
facts.says: The pee doesn't smell weird and he doesn't seem to be in pain when he goes.

facts.chart: Full-term birth, no NICU stay, no chronic medical conditions, growth and development normal to date
facts.says: He was born full-term, no problems, he's always been a healthy kid, no issues before this.

facts.chart: Usual diet is whole milk plus table foods; normally eats well, no feeding issues at baseline
facts.says: Normally he drinks whole milk and eats whatever we're eating, finger foods, he's a pretty good eater usually.

facts.chart: Sleep slightly disrupted by illness, waking more at night, otherwise normal baseline sleep
facts.says: He's been waking up more at night since this started, probably his tummy bothering him.

facts.chart: No siblings; no other household contacts currently ill
facts.says: It's just him, no brothers or sisters, and nobody else at home is sick right now.

facts.chart: Attends daycare 4 days per week while mother works as pharmacy technician
facts.says: He goes to daycare four days a week while I'm at work at the pharmacy.

facts.chart: Mother anxious about dehydration, searched symptoms online, wants reassurance about whether ER visit is needed
facts.says: I was up all night googling and I don't know if I should just take him to the ER or if this is something we can handle at home.

facts.chart: Gave one dose of children's acetaminophen (weight-appropriate) for fever yesterday evening, with some improvement
facts.says: I gave him a dose of the kids' Tylenol last night for the fever and that seemed to help a bit.

facts.chart: No recent travel, no new foods introduced recently
facts.says: We haven't traveled anywhere and I haven't given him anything new to eat.

facts.chart: No yellowing of skin or eyes noted
facts.says: His skin and eyes look normal, no yellow color or anything.

facts.chart: Fever and vomiting trending better today compared to yesterday; diarrhea still frequent but mother perceives slight improvement in consistency
facts.says: Today actually seems a little better than yesterday, the fever's lower and he's thrown up less, but the diarrhea is still pretty bad.

facts.chart: Mother hoping for guidance on fluids/feeding and whether in-person or ER evaluation is needed
facts.says: I just want to know what I should be feeding him and giving him to drink, and if I need to take him in somewhere today.

facts.chart: No smokers in household, no secondhand smoke exposure
facts.says: Nobody smokes in our house, so he's not around that.

facts.chart: Mother reports immunizations are up to date; she is not aware that the 12-month vaccines are outstanding.
facts.says: Oh, he's had all his shots, we never miss those.

mismatches.patientClaim: Mother says Mateo has 'had all his shots'.
mismatches.recordEvidence: The immunization record shows MMR, varicella and hepatitis B dose 3 have not been given; the well-child note from a week ago records them as deferred.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Caregivers often believe a child is fully immunized when doses are outstanding. Check the record rather than relying on recall, mention the gap without blame, and arrange catch-up once he has recovered. Completed rotavirus vaccination makes rotavirus less likely but does not exclude viral gastroenteritis.

mismatches.patientClaim: Mother believes diluted apple juice is a gentle, helpful fluid choice for her son's upset stomach
mismatches.recordEvidence: Weight trend and vitals flowsheet show continued weight loss (10.4kg to 10.1kg) and reduced urine output despite juice intake, consistent with juice being an inadequate/counterproductive rehydration fluid (high sugar content can worsen osmotic diarrhea)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Fruit juice, particularly apple juice, is a common but inappropriate home remedy for pediatric diarrhea; it does not provide adequate electrolyte replacement and can worsen diarrhea due to high fructose/sorbitol content. Oral rehydration solution is the appropriate alternative.

objectives.text: Elicit a focused history of acute gastroenteritis including onset, pattern of vomiting/diarrhea, exposures, and hydration status indicators from the caregiver
Perform a remote dehydration assessment using caregiver-guided exam maneuvers (skin turgor, mucous membranes, tears, capillary refill, mental status) and integrate with weight change

Elicit, through sensitive and non-judgmental direct questioning, an unsafe home medication practice (adult loperamide given to a toddler) that is not reflected in the chart, and provide clear counseling to correct it
Recognize and address a caregiver belief/practice mismatch regarding fluid choice (diluted juice, stopping milk) and provide correct oral rehydration guidance

Formulate an appropriate diagnosis of viral gastroenteritis with mild dehydration, differentiate from more concerning causes (e.g., intussusception, bacterial enteritis), and provide clear return precautions within the scope of a telehealth pediatric visit
Review growth and immunization records in context of an acute visit to confirm baseline health status and identify any care gaps to address at a future well visit

patient.name: Mateo Vargas
patient.appearance: On camera, Mateo is a round-cheeked toddler with dark curly hair, wearing a onesie, sitting on his mother's lap and intermittently fussing and reaching for a toy. His mother Camila, a young woman with her hair in a ponytail and visibly tired, holds him close and adjusts the camera periodically; they are in a softly lit living room with a diaper bag visible nearby.

persona.personality: Attentive, anxious but cooperative; wants to do right by her son and is open to guidance once she trusts the clinician is not judging her
persona.communicationStyle: Talks quickly when worried, gives clear timelines, needs gentle encouragement to disclose the loperamide dose, responds well to being asked directly and kindly
persona.emotionalState: Worried and a bit sleep-deprived, oscillating between calm reporting and anxious tangents about whether she should go to the ER
persona.background: Camila Vargas is 26, works as a pharmacy technician, and is Mateo's primary caregiver along with her partner who is at work today. She has some familiarity with medications from her job, which is part of why she felt comfortable giving an OTC product, though she now worries she may have done the wrong thing.
speechExamples: I've been up most of the night watching him, I just want to make sure I'm doing the right thing.
He's drinking a little, not a ton, but he's not refusing it either.
I work at a pharmacy so I know a bit about medicines, but now I'm second-guessing myself about something I gave him.
Should I just take him to urgent care, or is it okay to handle this from home?
He's cranky but when I hold him he settles down pretty quick.
concerns: Whether Mateo is dehydrated enough to need the ER or IV fluids
Whether the apple juice and stopping milk were the right calls
Guilt and worry about having given him adult diarrhea medicine
How to get him to drink more without force-feeding him
When he can go back to daycare

scenario.studentBrief: You are a pediatrics resident conducting a telehealth video visit. The patient is Mateo Vargas, a 14-month-old boy. His mother, Camila Vargas, is on the call holding him on her lap and will give the history on his behalf. The reason for the visit is vomiting and diarrhea over the past two days. Take a focused history from the mother, guide her through remote exam maneuvers as needed, assess hydration status, review the chart as appropriate, and develop a plan with teaching and clear return precautions.
scenario.chiefComplaint: 2 days of vomiting (improving) and watery diarrhea with low-grade fever in a 14-month-old
scenario.openingLine: Hi, thanks for seeing us - Mateo's been throwing up for a couple of days and now he's got really watery diarrhea, like six times a day. I'm worried he might be getting dehydrated.
tasks: Take a focused history of the presenting illness including exposures, fluid intake, and urine output
Guide the mother through remote assessment maneuvers (skin pinch, mucous membranes, tears, capillary refill)
Take a complete history of all medications and fluids given at home
Review the growth chart, recent vitals, and immunization record
Formulate a diagnosis, create a management plan, provide education, and give clear return precautions

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; mother and child at home in their living room
profile.summary: A 26-year-old mother brings her 14-month-old son to a telehealth visit for 2 days of vomiting (now improving) and frequent watery diarrhea with low-grade fever, after daycare exposure. The case teaches remote dehydration assessment, recognition of an unsafe home medication practice (adult loperamide given to a toddler) and an inappropriate fluid choice (diluted apple juice), and appropriate oral rehydration counseling within pediatric telehealth scope.
profile.title: Acute Vomiting and Diarrhea with Mild Dehydration in a 14-Month-Old
